name: Vasant Kearney
bio:
Vasant Kearney is founder and CEO of Onlay AI, where he builds agentic healthcare revenue-cycle infrastructure across claims, eligibility, attachments, payer follow-up, payment posting, and bank reconciliation.

He was previously co-founder and CTO of Retrace, an AI company focused on healthcare automation. Before startups, Vasant was an Assistant Professor of Radiation Oncology Physics at UCSF, completed a medical physics residency there, and earned a PhD in Biomedical Engineering. He mentored radiation oncology residents at UCSF and machine learning students at the University of San Francisco. His scientific work spans a broad range of topics, including generative MRI-to-CT translation, tumor localization, anatomy segmentation, treatment-planning optimization, NVIDIA CUDA programming, and dental disease classification.

His work sits at the intersection of healthcare operations, regulated workflows, multimodal AI, and production agent systems.

positions.claim: LLMs perform better when confined to strict, limited-vocabulary formats, which is why X12 works as a harness for claims agents.
Every step of the claim lifecycle has an X12 correspondence, so any agent action — phone call, portal, desktop, imaging system — can be reduced to a structured transaction.
An X12 response from an insurance company is not ground truth; the payer's portal, phone system, and X12 layer can all report the same wrong answer.
Teams should maintain their own internal X12 representation treated as correct only until downstream evidence disproves it.
Swapping in a newer, higher-scoring model can break a working system, so evals, testing, and validation must be rebuilt from scratch before the upgrade.
Enterprise healthcare agents should store memory in a database rather than on the local filesystem the way Claude Code and Codex do.
Persistent cross-session user memory introduces bias toward repeating yesterday's action, so users must be able to break out of it.
Fully hardcoding the claims workflow is not a viable alternative to agents because the codebase bloats and requires an oversized engineering team.
Collapsing an image into extracted findings before downstream modeling loses context that later procedures depend on, so processing should stay multimodal.
Public standard schemas are preferable to agent-generated schemas because they are lookup-able by both new engineers and coding agents.
Using an overpowered, expensive model for high-frequency routine transactions defeats the cost-reduction purpose of the system.
Agent failures should be attributed to system design rather than to model error.
